title: Free or defended: who can really recapture?
outcomes: Counts only the pieces that can capture on a square as its defenders
Decides whether a capture is free, wins points or loses points
Does not treat a nearby enemy piece as a defender

steps.text: In **Taking pieces: is the capture safe?** you learned to ask whether a piece is guarded. Now look closer. A piece is **loose** when it is attacked and nothing defends it. A defender counts only if it can capture on that very square with its own kind of move. A piece standing right next to the target proves nothing; count the pieces that actually attack the square.

steps.caption: The rook attacks the bishop on g5. The pawn on h6 defends it. The pawn on g6 stands in front of it but cannot capture on g5.

line.say: The rook takes the bishop for 3 points.
The h6 pawn recaptures. The g6 pawn could not have. White gave 5 for 3.

steps.text: So there are two questions. Is the square defended, by a piece that really attacks it? If it is, compare what you take with what you could lose. As a **rule of thumb**, with the counting values 1, 3, 3, 5, 9, a cheaper piece capturing a defended piece can still win points, and a dearer piece capturing a defended pawn loses them. The values are only a guide.

steps.title: Same capture, the defender changes
steps.prompt: Predict first: is the capture good when no piece defends the pawn, when a bishop defends it, and when a bishop stands nearby but cannot capture on that square?

Which kind of nearby piece fooled you most often: a piece of the wrong colour square, a pawn straight in front, or a rook behind a blocker? Name one square where you counted a defender that was not one.
